kicker: The village well — anyone can draw from it, but you need to know which water is clean.
summary: The open AI world is a village sharing its wells — learn to read the stone by the well and you can choose your water.

quiz.q: You plan to use a model downloaded from Hugging Face to make content for a client. Which line on the model card should you read first?
quiz.explain: The license decides whether you may use it commercially, change it or share it. Downloads only tell you the model is popular, not that you are allowed to use it.

wells.label: Two wells
wells.art: A moonlit night at the edge of the village: two mossy stone wells, each with a bamboo bucket. The left well's water glints with lines of code like fish scales; the right one holds small labelled clay jars. A paper lantern hangs from a wooden post between them.
wells.aria: Two wells: GitHub and Hugging Face. Put each item into the right well

wells.name: GitHub
wells.aria: GitHub well: where people share source code

wells.name: Hugging Face
wells.holds: the well of models, data, demos
wells.aria: Hugging Face well: where people share models, datasets and demos

wells.wrong: This one usually lives in the other well.

insight.text: Hugging Face is the shared well for models, datasets and demos — mostly public, free for anyone to download.

detail.text: GitHub is the well for source code: each repository holds code, files and the change history of every file.

wells.note: The line isn't absolute: GitHub also has downloadable files, and Hugging Face also holds code. This is enough to get started.

depth.label: A deepening well
depth.art: A cross-section of an old well unrolled like a scroll: rings of stone laid down over the years, the water rising notch by notch. The moon glides along the well's mouth; each notch has a small stone carved with a date. At the end of the scroll, white mist covers the mouth of the well.
depth.prompt: Drag the moon through the years
depth.aria: Progress tide: public models on Hugging Face over the years. Drag the moon or use the arrow keys

fact.text: In September 2024, Hugging Face co-founder Clément Delangue announced the hub had passed 1 million public models.
20 Feb 2026: the ggml team behind llama.cpp — the engine for running AI on personal computers — joined Hugging Face; both say it stays open source.
Hugging Face's Models page now lists over 3.15 million public models; over 211,000 have GGUF files for running on your own machine.

horizon.text: The well will probably keep getting deeper every year; knowing how to pick the right model will matter more than knowing many names.

insight.text: Today Hugging Face holds over 3.15 million public models — three times the 1 million mark of September 2024.

depth.detail: More choice also means more murky water. The skill you need: reading the stone by the well — the next scene.

card.label: Reading the well stone
card.art: Beside the well stands a low stone stele, six lines faintly carved under the moss. You hold a paper lantern; wherever it shines, a line becomes clear and casts its shadow on a puddle holding the moon.
card.prompt: Light each line on the stone
card.aria: A mock model card: six lines to read before you download a model
card.mock: A made-up model for learning, not a real one

lines.label: Name & author
lines.read: Who is the author, and do they have an official page? Is this the original, or someone else's copy or compressed version?

lines.label: Parameters
lines.read: Bigger usually means smarter but heavier. An ordinary laptop suits models of about 1B–14B (see the next station).

lines.label: License
lines.read: It decides whether you may use it commercially, change it or share it. “other” means you have to open the separate terms and read them.

lines.label: File format
lines.read: GGUF runs in LM Studio, Ollama and llama.cpp. “Q4” is a 4-bit compressed version, much lighter than the original.

lines.label: Downloads
lines.read: It shows the model is popular — not that it is safe or good.

lines.label: Limits & warnings
lines.value: Not well tested in Vietnamese; may get figures wrong
lines.read: A careful author says plainly where the model is weak. A stone that says nothing about limits is a sign to be wary.

insight.text: Every model comes with a model card: its purpose, limits, training data and evaluation results.

detail.text: The license shows right on the model page; if it says “other”, the author must give the name of and a link to the separate terms.

repo.label: Two houses
repo.art: Two wooden houses beside a stone path under the moon, almost identical. The left one has its lights on, a swept porch and a wooden board listing repairs; the right one has its door shut, cobwebs everywhere, and the name on its gate carved one stroke off.
repo.aria: Compare two GitHub repos on six signals, then choose the one to trust

signals.label: README
signals.what: The front page: what it does, how to install it, examples.

signals.label: Stars
signals.what: How many people bookmarked it: popularity, not a guarantee of safety.

signals.label: Forks
signals.what: Copies others made to change on their own. A fake repo is often a renamed copy.

signals.label: Issues
signals.what: Where people report bugs and ask questions. Recent replies mean someone still looks after it.

signals.label: Releases
signals.what: Published versions with notes. Downloading from here is safer than grabbing stray files.

signals.label: License
signals.what: With no license, by default you may not copy, change or distribute it.

values.readme: Copied from the original, plus a “quick installer” button

repo.pickAria: Choose repo {name} as the one to trust
repo.right: Right. The original has a history, someone looking after it, and a clear license.
repo.wrong: Look closely at the name: “rn” is pretending to be “m”. The stars are almost equal, but the history and the care are completely different.

insight.text: Attackers have cloned popular GitHub repos in bulk, slipped in malware and re-uploaded them under identical names.

detail.text: A repo without a license falls under default copyright: the author keeps all rights and you may not copy it freely.

clean.label: Filtering the water
clean.art: A bamboo filter under the well's spout: water runs through layers of gravel, sand and charcoal, each layer a numbered stone. At the bottom a clay bowl catches clear water holding the whole moon.
clean.aria: Stepping-stone path: the safe order for downloading a model or some code. Tap them in turn or use the number keys
clean.wrongHint: This layer comes later — the water hasn't passed the one before.

steps.label: Find the true source
steps.detail: Go to the author's or organisation's official page and follow the link from there.
steps.why: A renamed copy looks exactly like the original.

steps.label: Read the license and limits
steps.detail: Open the model card or README; check the license allows what you plan to do.
steps.why: Finding out you can't use it after downloading is wasted effort.

steps.label: Pick a safer format
steps.detail: Prefer safetensors or GGUF; avoid pickle files (.bin, .pt, .pkl) from strangers.
steps.why: A pickle file can run code the moment it is opened.

steps.label: Check the security scan
steps.detail: Hugging Face file pages show scan results; if a file is flagged, stop.
steps.why: Hugging Face itself says its scanner doesn't catch 100%.

steps.label: Download with a known app
steps.detail: Use LM Studio, Ollama or the official page — never run odd commands pasted from a forum.
steps.why: “Quick install” commands are malware's favourite road.

steps.label: Test with harmless data
steps.detail: At first, give it only sample content, not client documents.
steps.why: If something is off, nothing precious is lost.

insight.text: Pickle model files can run malicious code the moment they're opened; prefer safetensors or GGUF from trusted authors.

detail.text: In 2024 the security firm JFrog found models on Hugging Face hiding a backdoor that fired when the pickle file was loaded.

clean.note: GGUF and safetensors hold only data, so they are safer than pickle — but no format is perfectly safe: the right source still matters.

t31-hf-models.note: The page counter showed 3,156,130 public models when checked on 15 Oct 2026; filtering by the GGUF library showed 211,773 models. The numbers change daily.

t31-repo-confusion.title: Millions of Malicious Repositories Flood GitHub
t31-repo-confusion.note: Reports research on “repo confusion” by the security firm Apiiro: popular repos cloned, infected with malware and re-uploaded under the same name. Exact numbers are hard to count because repos are constantly deleted and re-uploaded.

t31-hf-pickle.title: Pickle Scanning
t31-hf-pickle.note: Explains why loading a pickle file can run arbitrary code; the Hub's scanner is “not 100% foolproof”.

t31-jfrog.title: Data Scientists Targeted by Malicious Hugging Face ML Models with Silent Backdoor
t31-jfrog.note: JFrog reported about 100 flagged models; according to Ars Technica, JFrog said about 10 were truly malicious and most of the rest were research experiments.
